desc:
Rearrange a binary tree into a right chain: a tree in which no node has a left child and every node's right child is the next node in the preorder traversal of the original tree. The root stays the root and no value changes; only the child links change.

How trees are given. There is no tree type here. A binary tree is passed (or returned) as an integer array in level-order (top to bottom, left to right), the same way LeetCode serialises trees. A missing child is written as -1, and every real node value is non-negative. The children of a missing node are not listed, and trailing -1 entries are dropped, so a non-empty array never ends with -1. The empty tree is [].

For example, [1, 2, 3, -1, 4] describes the tree below: the root is 1 with children 2 and 3, node 2 has no left child and has 4 as its right child, and node 3 is a leaf.

    1
   / \
  2   3
   \
    4

Return the flattened tree in the same level-order encoding. For tree = [1, 2, 5, 3, 4, -1, 6] the preorder is 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, so the answer is [1, -1, 2, -1, 3, -1, 4, -1, 5, -1, 6]. The empty tree stays [].
constraints: Every tree array follows the encoding above exactly (valid level-order, no trailing -1)
hints: Write down the preorder of the tree first. The flattened tree is a chain through exactly these nodes in this order.
What does the level-order encoding of a right chain with values v1, v2, ..., vn look like? Each node contributes its value and then a -1 for its missing left child.
Do a preorder traversal with an explicit stack (push the right child, then the left child, so the left one is popped first) and output value, -1 for each node. Remove the final trailing -1.
editorial: The flattened tree is determined entirely by the preorder of the original: the chain visits the nodes in preorder, so the problem reduces to computing the preorder traversal and then writing a chain in level-order encoding. A chain with values v1, ..., vn is the array v1, -1, v2, -1, ..., vn because every node has a missing left child but its right child is listed next.

To flatten the tree in place, as it is usually asked in interviews, you would instead splice each left subtree between a node and its right subtree: for a node, find the last node of its left subtree (the rightmost one), attach the node's old right subtree there, move the left subtree to the right and clear the left link. Both approaches run in linear time; the preorder one needs O(n) memory for the stack, the splicing one (Morris style) only O(1).
